claim: For typical Boolean target functions, transformers trained on inputs with feature noise fail to learn the noiseless function, because the best predictor under noise is less sensitive to input flips than the target, and transformers' bias toward low-sensitivity functions draws them to that simpler predictor. Supported only if, for thousands of random sparse Boolean functions (juntas), the optimal noisy predictor's sensitivity never exceeds the target's and transformers' noiseless accuracy falls as the sensitivity gap grows while their noisy validation error stays near optimal with little overfitting; if, on a constructed trap function whose optimal noisy predictor is about as accurate as the target but much less sensitive, transformers converge to the trap while LSTMs fail by memorising the training set; and if adding a loss term that rewards sensitivity lets transformers learn the target at a well-chosen penalty weight but does not help when the optimal noisy predictor is much more accurate than the target (Maj(30,4)).

experiments: Define noise-robust learning. Setup: uniform random bitstrings X, label Y = f(X), inputs corrupted by independent bit flips with probability p (labels never flipped); models are trained and validated on noisy pairs (Z, Y) and judged by accuracy on noiseless X. The Bayes-optimal noisy predictor is f* = sign(T_{1-2p} f), with T the noise operator; its error is bounded above and below by functions of H(Y|Z). Sensitivity sens[f] = sum over bits of the probability that flipping that bit changes f. Majority over an odd number of bits and parity are their own optimal noisy predictors (Proposition 1); for a uniformly random function, E[sens f*] ~ (n/pi) arccos(2p(1-p) / (p^2 + (1-p)^2)) < E[sens f] for p in (0, 1/2] (Proposition 2).

Fix models and training. Setup: encoder-only transformers (depth 1-6, width 16-128, 2-8 heads, dropout 0.05-0.1, absolute positions) and LSTMs (depth 1-6, hidden 16-128), Xavier init, cross-entropy, up to 1,000 epochs with early stopping after 300 epochs without validation improvement, model taken at best validation accuracy. Hyperparameter ranges are pruned on noiseless runs until at least about 70% of models learn the noiseless function, so failures under noise are not capacity failures; 300 runs with random initialisation and hyperparameters per noise rate; median parameter count about 32.5k (transformer) and 46.5k (LSTM) on parity.

Test random sparse functions. Setup: 3,200 random k-juntas (k in {5, 6, 7}) on 10 bits with noise rates sampled from 0-0.30 (below about 0.10, f* = f with high probability), 5,000 training and 10,000 validation examples. Result: every sampled function has sens[f] >= sens[f*]; transformers succeed only when the sensitivity gap and the noisy-error gap between f and f* are both near zero, and noiseless accuracy worsens as the sensitivity gap grows, while final validation error is near the optimum and train and validation error are close (histograms). The authors note the noisy-error gap grows together with the sensitivity gap, which confounds this correlation.

Separate simplicity bias from loss minimisation with a trap function. Setup: search weight-based functions for n in 4-8 and p in 0.20-0.30 for one where err(f*) ~ err(f) but sens[f*] << sens[f]; 19 runs each of transformers, LSTMs, and transformers with an extra loss term approximating -lambda * sens[f_hat]; also on Maj(30,4). Result: on the trap, transformers move toward the low-sensitivity optimal predictor and reach near-optimal noisy validation accuracy, while LSTMs end near a lookup table of the training data; all models sit in a 0.5-0.6 noisy-accuracy band; with lambda = 1 transformers learn the true function, and accuracy has a clear optimum in lambda; on Maj(30,4) the penalty has minimal effect.

Note the scope. Setup: noise is independent, identical bit flips on uniform inputs; the authors argue independent but non-identical noise should preserve sens[f*] <= sens[f], but correlated flips can raise the sensitivity of the smoothed function, so the conclusion need not hold for correlated noise; the effect needs noise rates high enough that f* != f, which may be rare in natural data; tasks are small synthetic Boolean functions with tiny models. Results are reported as distributions over random hyperparameters rather than a single tuned model, and the sensitivity-penalty success depends on a narrowly tuned lambda.
